newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic foes look to unions, foreign pressure. [CORRECTED 00:51 GMT 12/12]
newsitem.headline: Milosevic foes look to unions, foreign pressure. [CORRECTED 00:51 GMT 12/12]

text.p: The Yugoslav opposition is pinning its hopes on union backing and growing international support in its battle for control of town councils amid signs that support for its rallies is starting to fade.
Crowds appeared to be declining in the past few days, but in Belgrade on Wednesday (corrects) they also included the first organised group of workers since the daily street protests began.
The United States and European Parliament both fired warning shots across Milosevic's bows, threatening unspecified measures if he uses force to put down the daily opposition marches in Belgrade.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told CBS television that if Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic continued his "repressive, undemocratic stance" he would doom his hopes of ties to the West.
"He really is turning his back on opportunities to join the West, which I know is important to him," Christopher said.
He said the United States was considering reintroducing economic sanctions. The United Nations imposed sanctions on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years for its role in the war in Bosnia.
The huge protest marches began after Milosevic's socialist government annulled opposition victories in local elections 25 days ago.
The European Parliament added its voice, issuing a strongly-worded statement expressing deep concern about developments in Yugoslavia.
EU foreign ministers on December 6 postponed a decision to offer Yugoslavia preferential trade terms already granted to other Balkan states.

Diplomatic sources said those messages were likely to be forcefully repeated in private when Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini meets Milosevic and Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic on Thursday.
"I am going to Belgrade to assess the situation in the hope that I can make a contribution to resolving the crisis under way," Dini told reporters in Milan on Wednesday evening.
Diplomatic sources said the mission had the backing of NATO and that the United States had been informed.

The U.S. had earlier cancelled a meeting with Milosevic and its Balkans negotiator John Kornblum in an attempt to isolate the president over the crisis, and it was not imediately clear if Washington supported Dini's Belgrade trip.
But political analysts said the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition would look to the rising foreign pressure to help revive apparently flagging interest in the marches.
Zajedno has been able to draw crowds of up to 150,000, but over the past few days the numbers have appeared to decline as the marches settled into a predictable routine with few new developments.

Observers estimated that about 80,000 people attended Wednesday's demonstration, while in the industrial town of Nis the independent Fonet news agency reported barely one tenth of the usual crowd joined the march.
Leaders of the association of independent trade unions said some 10,000 workers had been taking part in the daily student and opposition rallies.
"We were also here before (as individuals) but for the first time today we are here in an organised way," association president Rade Radovanovic told Reuters.
Thousands of workers marched behind a trade union banner in a show of unity that Radovanovic earlier said would shake Milosevic and his deputies.
Independent unions claimed some of their 40,000 members in Belgrade had begun strike action citing the alleged election fraud among their grievances along with demands for pay.
"It is an old communist belief that when the workers come out against you, you are finished," he said.
